definition: Most noticeable or important in a particular context.
example: The most salient difference between the plans was their ongoing cost.
nuance: Salient is context-dependent: a fact can be salient for one decision and irrelevant to another.
prompt: A briefing highlights the facts that matter most to the decision.
options: She summarized the salient findings before discussing minor details.
Every incidental detail was equally salient, with nothing standing out.
The findings were salient because they had remained hidden for years.
The analyst stayed salient through the whole briefing, never saying a word.
reasons: This sentence demonstrates the meaning: most noticeable or important in a particular context.
Salience distinguishes what stands out from incidental details.
Being hidden is not being noticeable or prominent.
This confuses the word with silent; it describes what stands out, not someone keeping quiet.

practice.prompt: A birdwatcher explains to a friend how to recognize a rare warbler.
options: The salient warbler cleverly figured out how to open the latched feeder.
The salient mark of this warbler is the bright yellow patch on its throat.
The warbler's salient markings blend into the leaves so well that nobody spots them.
Its salient feature is that it looks exactly like every other small brown bird.
reasons: This treats the word as meaning clever, mixing it up with sapient.
A vivid patch that catches the eye is exactly what helps someone pick out the bird.
Markings that vanish against the leaves are the opposite of eye-catching.
Looking like every other bird gives the friend nothing distinctive to look for.
